anchor_text: no man living shall come over it
summary: Benedick says he will write Margaret a sonnet so lofty 'no man living shall come over it.' Margaret seizes on 'come over' as a sexual double meaning (to mount or have sex with) and replies with a second pun: to 'keep below stairs' means both to stay on the ground floor (social inferiority) and to remain underneath in the sexual act. The rapid exchange establishes the scene's tone of sexual combat.
detail: The pun on 'come over' (to surmount, or to have sex with) was current in Elizabethan slang; Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'over,' notes the sexual sense in several plays. Margaret's retort 'shall I always keep below stairs?' extends the double meaning: 'below stairs' denotes the servant's quarter (she is Hero's waiting-gentlewoman) and simultaneously the sexual position. The exchange belongs to a long scene of fencing-metaphor banter that follows, where 'bucklers,' 'swords,' and 'pikes' carry the same double register. Margaret here plays Benedick's equal in wit, ironically echoing the Beatrice-Benedick 'merry war.'

Both registers of the pun are cleanly supported by the text: Benedick's 'come over it' prompts Margaret's immediate deflection to 'keep below stairs,' which works simultaneously as servant-quarters self-deprecation and as a sexual-position joke; the reading is mainstream and unforced.

anchor_text: give thee the bucklers
summary: Benedick surrenders the verbal duel by saying 'I give thee the bucklers' (I yield the shield; I concede), using fencing language. Margaret parries: 'Give us the swords, we have bucklers of our own' — claiming women have their own defensive weapon. Benedick then warns the 'pikes' in their bucklers are 'dangerous weapons for maids,' turning the shield's central spike (a literal pike) into a phallic joke about female chastity.
detail: A buckler was a small round shield carried in the left hand; its centre held a metal spike called the pike or boss. In fencing, 'giving the bucklers' meant yielding the match. 'Give us the swords' reverses the surrender: Margaret claims the women need no male shield because they have their own. Benedick's warning that the pikes must be 'put in with a vice' (forced in with a screw) and are 'dangerous weapons for maids' turns the pike into a phallus — maids (virgins) are at risk. The passage is a sustained fencing-as-sex conceit. Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'buckler' and 'pike,' confirms both the fencing terminology and the bawdy valence.

anchor_text: Leander the good swimmer, Troilus the first employer of panders
summary: Benedick lines up the two most famous lovers in classical legend as his superiors in love. Leander swam the Hellespont every night to reach his beloved Hero; when he drowned, Hero threw herself from her tower. Troilus sent his love-messages to Cressida through a go-between named Pandarus — making Troilus, Benedick jokes, 'the first employer of panders' (the origin of the word 'pander,' a procurer of love). Benedick claims to surpass them both in the depth of his suffering.
detail: Leander's nightly swim of the Hellespont was the subject of Marlowe's Hero and Leander (printed 1598, close to Much Ado's composition), drawing on Ovid's Heroides 18-19 and the Greek poem of Musaeus. Benedick's flat epithet 'the good swimmer' deflates the legend's tragic grandeur into a talent-show item. Troilus's go-between Pandarus is the source of the English verb 'to pander' (to procure, to supply another's desires). The list of 'quondam carpet-mongers' — former bedroom-lurkers, men known only for their love-affairs — mocks the convention of citing classical precedent for one's passions, which Benedick simultaneously enacts. The phrase 'run smoothly in the even road of a blank verse' is a dig at the mechanical blank-verse love-complaint: Benedick cannot write that way.

anchor_text: for 'scorn,' 'horn', a hard rime
summary: Benedick cannot find a rhyme for 'scorn' except 'horn,' which he calls 'a hard rime' — both because it does not rhyme cleanly and because 'horn' is the emblem of the cuckold, the man whose wife is unfaithful. He is trying to write a love-poem and cannot escape the Elizabethan joke that every marriage ends with the husband wearing invisible horns. 'Fool' for 'school' likewise implies he is a fool to be in love.
detail: The cuckold's 'horns' were a fixed joke: a married man whose wife slept with another man was said to grow invisible horns on his forehead, the mark of his dishonour. Benedick, the confirmed bachelor who swore never to marry for fear of the 'yoke' and the 'horn' (1.1), cannot write a love-sonnet without the rhyme-scheme ambushing him with the cuckoldry joke. 'Horn' / 'scorn' is not a full rhyme in modern pronunciation but was closer in Elizabethan English. The sequence 'baby / lady... horn / scorn... fool / school' turns the attempt to write Petrarchan love-verse into a confession of all the reasons against love. For the horn-cuckold tradition, see Elizabethan proverbial lore; OED s.v. 'horn,' sense 6.

anchor_text: erect in this age his own tomb ere he dies
summary: Benedick argues that a man must praise himself in 'this age' because no one else will remember him: if he does not 'erect his own tomb' (build his own memorial) before dying, he will be forgotten as quickly as the funeral bell stops ringing and the widow's tears dry. Wealthy Elizabethans paid for elaborate memorial tombs and brass inscriptions in parish churches precisely to ensure their names survived; Benedick claims that without doing so yourself, your memory lasts only an hour and a quarter.
detail: Elaborate self-funded funerary monuments — altar tombs, brass effigies, painted epitaphs — were a real and costly Elizabethan practice; parish churches across England are still full of them. The assumption was that money or verse could 'erect' a monument to one's name that outlasted the grave. Shakespeare engages seriously with this topos in Sonnets 55 ('Not marble, nor the gilded monuments / Of princes shall outlive this powerful rhyme') and 18 ('So long as men can breathe, or eyes can see, / So long lives this'). Benedick's comic version reduces the meditation on immortality to a timetable: one hour of church-bell and fifteen minutes of widow-weeping. 'In monument' = in memorialized form; 'the bell rings' refers to the passing-bell tolled at funerals.

anchor_text: live in thy heart, die in thy lap
summary: Benedick's farewell plays on a conventional Elizabethan sexual double meaning: 'die' was slang for orgasm, and 'lap' for the female genitals (as Hamlet uses it at Ophelia's lap in 3.2). The line works on two levels: a sentimental declaration of devotion (to live in her affection, to die loved by her, to be buried in the memory of her eyes) and an innuendo-laced promise of sexual intimacy. The joke immediately deflates into the practical 'and moreover I will go with thee to thy uncle's.'
detail: The Elizabethan meaning of 'to die' as sexual climax is well attested; Donne, Sidney, and Nashe all exploit it in verse. 'Lap' as female genitalia is used by Shakespeare in Hamlet 3.2 ('Lady, shall I lie in your lap? ... Do you think I meant country matters?'). The tricolon 'live in thy heart, die in thy lap, and be buried in thy eyes' is a conceit structured as birth-life-death (heart = emotional life, lap = physical consummation, eyes = memorial), but the middle term's sexual charge undercuts the sentiment. Benedick's immediate pivot — 'and moreover I will go with thee to thy uncle's' — is the comic deflation that signals his discomfort with high sentiment, the same habit that makes him undercut his own love-verses in the preceding speech.

anchor_text: Death, in guerdon of her wrongs
summary: 'Guerdon' means reward or recompense. Claudio's epitaph argues that Death, as payment for the wrong done to Hero by slander, gives her an undying fame — her reputation outlasts her supposed disgrace.
detail: The word entered English from Old French 'guerdon' (itself from a Germanic root); it was already archaic and literary in Shakespeare's day, lending the epitaph a heightened, formal register. Onions (Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'guerdon') glosses it simply as 'reward, recompense.' The argument of the verse follows the classical consolatio pattern: temporal suffering yields eternal glory.

anchor_text: Pardon, goddess of the night, Those that slew thy virgin knight
summary: 'Goddess of the night' is Diana (Greek Artemis), goddess of the moon and of chastity. Hero is called her 'virgin knight' because she was a chaste, unmarried girl — a member, so to speak, of Diana's company of virgins. The mourners beg Diana's pardon for those whose slander 'slew' her.
detail: In classical mythology Diana presided over the moon, the hunt, and, above all, chastity; she and her band of virgin nymphs were the type of female purity. Ovid describes her in the Metamorphoses as the fierce guardian of that purity (the story of Actaeon, who glimpsed her bathing, ends in his death). Calling Hero a 'virgin knight' is a chivalric overlay on the classical idea: she served Diana's cause of chastity, and was destroyed for a false charge against that very virtue. The song thus casts Claudio and Don Pedro as those who 'slew' Diana's devotee — the accusation is their own guilt, not Hero's. The same Diana-as-chastity-goddess figures in the play at 4.1, when Leonato laments that his daughter should have been 'the daughter of a goddess' — the language picks up this same cult of the virgin deity.

anchor_text: Before the wheels of Phoebus, round about Dapples the drowsy east with spots of grey
summary: Phoebus is the sun-god (Apollo in his role as the sun), imagined driving a chariot across the sky. 'Before the wheels of Phoebus' means just before sunrise — the eastern sky is brightening ahead of the chariot. Don Pedro uses the image to signal that dawn has come and the night-vigil at the tomb is over.
detail: The sun-chariot is among the most persistent images in classical poetry: Ovid's Metamorphoses, Golding's 1567 translation, and a dozen other texts describe Phoebus (Apollo) harnessing his fire-breathing horses each morning to drive the sun from east to west. 'Phoebus' (Greek for 'the bright') was the standard Elizabethan literary name for the sun-god in this driving function, as distinct from Apollo as god of music and prophecy. 'Dapples' captures the patchy grey-and-pink of predawn light; the word is Shakespeare's own contribution to the visual detail. The transition from torchlight-vigil to natural daylight also marks the shift from mourning to hope: the next scene brings the wedding.

Phoebus's sun-chariot as a marker of imminent dawn is a stock classical image that fits the line exactly; the structural reading — torchlight vigil gives way to daylight and the shift from mourning to hope — is the plain dramatic logic of the scene's ending.

anchor_text: Hymen now with luckier issue speed's
summary: Hymen was the classical god of marriage, invoked at weddings; his name stood for the wedding ceremony itself. Claudio prays that Hymen will bring his next marriage a happier outcome ('luckier issue') than the disaster that 'this' one — Hero's supposed death — brought about. The prayer signals that the comedy's resolution is now imminent.
detail: In Greek and Roman poetry Hymen (or Hymenaeus) was invoked at the start of the wedding procession; his name appears in the traditional wedding cry 'O Hymen, Hymenaee!' (as in Catullus 61). 'Issue' here means outcome or result, not offspring. Claudio's phrasing is pointed: the disastrous 'issue' of the first betrothal (Hero publicly shamed, apparently dead, the wedding wrecked) is placed against the hoped-for 'luckier' outcome of this new one. Since the audience knows Hero is alive, the line is dramatically ironic — the 'luckier issue' will prove to be the same woman he wronged. Shakespeare uses Hymen as a speaking character in As You Like It (5.4), presiding over the multiple marriages there.

sources.name: Catullus, Carmina

Hymen as the god of marriage is uncontroversial; glossing 'issue' as outcome rather than offspring is the correct contextual reading, and the dramatic-irony observation (the 'luckier issue' will prove to be the same woman Claudio wronged) is mainstream and well-supported by the play's resolution.

anchor_text: by faith enforc'd / To call young Claudio to a reckoning
summary: 'Call to a reckoning' means to demand satisfaction or challenge to a duel: if the truth about Hero had not come out, Benedick would have been honour-bound to fight Claudio for the wrong done to Beatrice's cousin. The phrase captures how close the comedy came to tragedy.
detail: In Elizabethan usage a 'reckoning' is literally a settling of accounts, and to 'call a man to a reckoning' is to demand he answer for an injury — most commonly at sword-point. Benedick's willingness to challenge his close friend Claudio (at Beatrice's insistence: 'Kill Claudio,' 4.1) is the moral hinge of his character: he chooses love and justice over male camaraderie. That the challenge is now unnecessary, not that it was wrong, is the comedy's resolution.

The gloss is sound: 'call to a reckoning' as demanding satisfaction or a duel is well-attested Elizabethan usage, and the annotation correctly locates the dramatic stakes — Benedick's willingness to challenge Claudio is the moral pivot of his character arc.

anchor_text: with confirm'd countenance
summary: 'Confirm'd countenance' means a steady, composed expression — a face that will not betray surprise or hesitation. Antonio promises to present the masked Hero to Claudio as if she were simply his niece, without flinching.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, Alexander, Shakespeare-Lexicon (3rd ed., 1902), s.v. 'confirmed': 'settled, firm, resolute'; s.v. 'countenance': 'look, expression of face.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2147
Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon does carry 'confirmed' (settled, firm, resolute) and 'countenance' (look, expression) as standard entries; both senses and the citation are accurate.

A straightforward archaic-vocabulary gloss; 'confirmed countenance' meaning a steady, composed expression is defensible from the context — Antonio is undertaking a theatrical deception and must not give the game away.

anchor_text: To bind me, or undo me; one of them
summary: Benedick plays on two meanings: the Friar will either 'bind' him in the marriage ceremony (formally join him to Beatrice) or 'undo' him by refusing and leaving him still tormented by love. 'Undo' also carries the sense of ruining or unmaking him as the confirmed bachelor he once was.
detail: The joke is the signature Benedick move: he frames the greatest comic reversal of his life (the sworn woman-hater agreeing to marry) in a mock-legalistic dilemma, as if the Friar were judge rather than officiant. 'Bind' also recalls the contractual language of betrothal — to be 'bound' to another — while 'undo' echoes the frequent Elizabethan sense of being destroyed or unmade. His pose of reluctance is undercut by the fact that he has just formally declared his love to Leonato.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'bind' v. 5: 'to unite by a tie of duty, obligation, or affection'; s.v. 'undo' v. 3a: 'to bring to ruin or destruction, to ruin.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2150
OED records 'bind' in the sense of uniting by moral or affectional tie and 'undo' in the sense of bringing to ruin; both senses are well-attested and support the annotation's claims.

Both senses of 'bind' (join in matrimony / legally bind) and 'undo' (destroy the bachelor self / ruin him by refusal) are active in the line; the mock-legalistic framing is characteristic of Benedick's wit and is accurately described.

anchor_text: were she an Ethiope
summary: 'Ethiope' (Ethiopian) was used by Elizabethan writers as a byword for dark-skinned beauty judged by European standards as the opposite of the fair complexion prized in Renaissance love poetry. Claudio means he will keep his word even if the woman turns out to be, in his culture's terms, as unlike the ideal of beauty as possible.

sources.name: Geneva Bible 1599
sources.citation: Song of Solomon (Canticles) 1:5 (Geneva 1599): 'I am black, but comely' — the 'black but beautiful' topos behind the period's habit of equating 'fair' with beautiful.

sources.name: Virgil, Eclogues
sources.citation: Virgil, Eclogues 2.16-18 ('quamvis ille niger... O formose puer, nimium ne crede colori') — a classical precedent weighing dark against fair complexion.

anchor_text: the savage bull. Tush! fear not, man, we'll tip thy horns with gold, / And all Europa shall rejoice at thee, / As once Europa did at lusty Jove
summary: Claudio alludes to Zeus (Roman Jupiter/Jove), who disguised himself as a white bull to abduct the princess Europa — so Benedick the 'savage bull' who is tamed by marriage will wear golden horns, just as 'lusty Jove' played the bull for love. The compliment is also a cuckold-joke: gilded horns are the comic emblem of the husband whose wife is unfaithful.
detail: The story: Zeus, infatuated with the Phoenician princess Europa, transformed himself into a beautiful white bull. She climbed on his back, and he carried her across the sea to Crete, where she bore him Minos, Rhadamanthus, and Sarpedon. Ovid tells the story at Metamorphoses 2.836-875. Claudio's pun is layered: 'tip thy horns with gold' both flatters Benedick by comparing him to divine Jove and simultaneously marks him as a future cuckold, since golden horns are the visible badge of the betrayed husband. Much Ado runs this horn-joke from the first act to the last.

sources.name: Ovid, Metamorphoses
sources.citation: Ovid, Metamorphoses 2.836-875 (Jove as bull abducting Europa); Arthur Golding's English translation, 1567.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2173

Ovid Metamorphoses 2.833-875 is the confirmed span for the Europa abduction; the annotation cites '2.836-875', placing the start three lines too late — a minor but real error in line numbering that falls within the scene-transition passage, making the citation slightly inaccurate.

The Europa/Jove myth is correctly glossed and the layered pun (gilded horns = divine compliment and cuckold emblem) is well established in the scholarship; the annotation does not over-reach and the Ovid locus (Met. 2.836-875) is accurate.

anchor_text: Bull Jove, sir, had an amiable low: / And some such strange bull leap'd your father's cow, / And got a calf in that same noble feat, / Much like to you, for you have just his bleat
summary: Benedick retaliates: 'Jove the bull had a charming moo — and some bull just like him mounted your father's cow and produced you, a calf.' 'Amiable low' = a loveable moo; 'cow' = Claudio's mother; 'calf' = fool (Claudio); 'bleat' = foolish cry. The joke accuses Claudio's mother of the same infidelity the men fear in wives, making Claudio the son of a cuckold.

The bawdy logic — Benedick redirects Claudio's Europa joke into an accusation of maternal adultery, making Claudio himself a calf (dolt) sired by a bull-god — is fully supported by the text, and the lexical glosses ('low' = moo, 'calf' = fool) are standard; however, the annotation's final aside that 'bleat' demotes Claudio from calf to lamb is a minor stretch since 'calf' does bleat, but it does not distort the reading.

anchor_text: One Hero died defil'd, but I do live, / And surely as I live, I am a maid
summary: Hero speaks of herself in the third person: the 'Hero' who was publicly shamed and driven to (apparent) death was defiled in name and reputation, not in body. She insists she is still 'a maid' — a virgin — the single fact on which her social existence depends. The Friar's plan allowed the slandered identity to die so the true one could be restored.
detail: Hero's riddling language ('another Hero,' 'when I liv'd, I was your other wife') echoes the Friar's plot from 4.1: by letting the world believe her dead, she allowed the false 'Hero' — the unchaste woman Claudio thought he saw — to bear the shame and perish, leaving the real Hero's innocence intact. The word 'defiled' is precise: it means sexually impure, and in this culture one such accusation, true or false, was a form of social death. Hero's assertion 'I am a maid' is both the legal fact that clears her and the emotional climax the play has been building toward. The scene does not dwell on Claudio's guilt or offer full apology; the comedy requires quick resolution.

sources.name: Vives, Instruction of a Christian Woman
sources.citation: Juan Luis Vives, De institutione feminae christianae (1523), trans. Richard Hyrde (1529): the Renaissance equation of a woman's honour with her chastity, discussed in relation to Much Ado by Carol Thomas Neely, Broken Nuptials in Shakespeare's Plays (1985), ch. 2.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2194

Vives, De institutione feminae christianae (1523), translated by Richard Hyrde (c.1529), is a real and well-documented Renaissance treatise on female chastity and honour; Carol Thomas Neely's Broken Nuptials (1985) is a genuine secondary source connecting Vives to Much Ado.

The annotation accurately captures Hero's riddling self-split and correctly glosses 'defiled' as sexually impure in a social-death sense; the note that the comedy requires quick resolution rather than dwelling on Claudio's guilt is an honest, mainstream critical observation rather than a distortion.

anchor_text: A halting sonnet of his own pure brain, / Fashion'd to Beatrice
summary: 'Halting' means limping — the verse scans badly, with irregular metre. Claudio mocks Benedick as a failed Petrarchan lover: he has tried to write a love sonnet to Beatrice in the fashionable mode but produced something technically clumsy. 'Pure brain' ('from his very own head') sharpens the joke: he wrote it himself, with no help.
detail: A 'halting' line in Elizabethan prosody is one that does not scan smoothly — it 'limps' (the root sense of 'halt'). The sonnet was the established form for addressing an idealized beloved, popularised by Petrarch and his English imitators (Sidney, Spenser). That Benedick, the champion sceptic of love poetry, has now produced a bad one is the play's ultimate comic proof of his transformation. Hero simultaneously produces Beatrice's poem — so both sworn anti-lovers have been secretly writing verses and both are equally bad at it. The scene performs the title pun: they are caught out by what they wrote, 'noted' in their own hands.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'halting' adj. 1b: 'of verse: that limps, imperfect in metre'; s.v. 'fashion' v. 2: 'to make, frame, compose.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2220
OED records 'halting' in the sense of metrically imperfect or limping verse, and 'fashion' in the sense of composing or framing; both senses are well-attested and directly support the annotation.

The core gloss ('halting' = metrically limping) is correct and well-attested, but the detail claim that the scene 'performs the title pun' — that they are 'noted' in their own hands — is a critical reading of the play's Nothing/Noting wordplay that, while argued by some scholars, is not unambiguously present in this passage and risks importing a thematic overlay not securely grounded in TLN 2220-2221 alone.

anchor_text: our own hands against our hearts
summary: 'Hands against our hearts': their handwriting (what their hands wrote) contradicts what their mouths have been saying ('our hearts' = their professed indifference). The contrast of hand/heart is an antithesis — and also a legal metaphor: a signed document ('our own hands') is the court evidence that overrules their verbal denials.
detail: In Elizabethan legal and epistolary usage 'one's hand' is one's signature or handwriting — a binding testimony. Benedick plays the scene as if a lawsuit has been decided against them: they have been their own witnesses to their love, in their own writing, and must accept the verdict. The antithesis (hands vs. hearts; writing vs. professed feeling) also neatly encapsulates the play's central device of 'noting': what is observed or recorded always tells more truth than what the characters claim to feel.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'hand' n. 12a: 'a person's handwriting, esp. as a legal signature or autograph'; s.v. 'against' prep. 8: 'in opposition to, contrary to.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2225
OED 'hand' n. 12a (handwriting, legal signature) is a genuine and well-documented sense; the legal-epistolary framing of 'one's hand' as binding testimony is accurate for the period.

The legal/epistolary sense of 'hand' as handwriting or signature is standard and confirmed by the dramatic situation (Claudio produces a paper 'written in his hand'); the antithesis of hands/hearts is accurately described as Benedick's mock-legal framing of comic capitulation.

anchor_text: cudgelled thee out of thy single life, to make thee a double-dealer
summary: 'Double-dealer' has two meanings at once: on the surface it means a married man (one who now deals with two people — himself and a wife), but it also means a cheat or deceiver, and specifically a man who cheats on his wife. Claudio's joke is that marriage will inevitably make Benedick unfaithful — unless Beatrice watches him very closely.
detail: The pun is clinched by 'out of question, thou wilt be, if my cousin do not look exceeding narrowly to thee' — Claudio bets Benedick will be unfaithful unless Beatrice keeps strict watch. 'Single' = unmarried (but also undivided, faithful to one); 'double' = married (two people) but also duplicitous. The joke recycles the play's endemic cuckoldry anxiety: even as it celebrates two weddings, the comedy cannot help implying that husbands cheat. Claudio's use of the cudgel-image ('beat you out of bachelorhood') also has a faintly aggressive edge — he is settling the score for Benedick's earlier threat to challenge him.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'double-dealer' n. 1: 'one who deals doubly or deceitfully'; s.v. 'single' adj. 10: 'unmarried, celibate.'

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, Alexander, Shakespeare-Lexicon (3rd ed., 1902), s.v. 'double-dealer': 'a cheat, one who acts a double part.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2241
OED 'double-dealer' n. 1 (one who acts deceitfully) and Schmidt's entry for 'double-dealer' as a cheat are both genuine; OED 'single' adj. 10 (unmarried) is also well-attested.

Both meanings of 'double-dealer' (married man dealing with two / deceitful cheat) are active in the text and confirmed by the continuation 'if my cousin do not look exceeding narrowly to thee'; the annotation does not over-read by also noting the cudgel-image as faintly aggressive score-settling, which is plausible but not asserted as certain.

anchor_text: no staff more reverent than one tipped with horn
summary: Benedick closes with one more cuckold-horn joke: a 'staff tipped with horn' is on the surface a walking stick with a horn ferrule (tip), an image of dignified old age. But 'horn' also means the cuckold's invisible horns, so the marriage-staff — the dignified prop of the married man — is permanently tipped with the mark of potential betrayal. The joke is his farewell to bachelor wit.
detail: A staff was a mark of authority and age — the bishop's crozier, the marshal's baton, the old man's cane — and 'reverent' (respected, venerable) belongs to that register. Benedick's mock-wisdom is that the most honourable staff a man can carry is one 'horned' by marriage, i.e. marked by the risk of cuckoldry. The joke caps a scene that has been threading horn-images from Claudio's 'tip thy horns with gold' through the bull/calf exchange, ending with Benedick himself wearing the comic crown. He is at once the hornwearer and the wit who names the joke: the play lets him face the anxiety by laughing at it. 'Tipped with horn' is also mildly phallic, adding a further bawdy layer.

sources.name: OED

OED 'tip' v.1 3 (to furnish with an end-piece) and 'reverent' adj. 1 (venerable) are real entries; Onions records 'horn' as the imaginary horn of a cuckold, a standard and well-documented Elizabethan usage.

The surface sense (a walking stick tipped with a horn ferrule as symbol of dignified age) and the cuckold-horn pun are both well-grounded; the additional claim that 'tipped with horn' is 'mildly phallic' is a stretch that lacks textual warrant in this specific phrase and is tagged at scholar depth only, which mitigates the risk.
